headline: This law updates the Packers and Stockyards Act so online and electronic livestock sales are clearly covered as marketing agency activity, with a $250,000 annual threshold, and allows electronic payment methods for prompt payment.
what_it_does: The law changes the definition of "marketing agency" in the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921 to include anyone who buys or sells livestock for a commission or fee using online, video, or other electronic methods. It exempts anyone whose average yearly electronic livestock sales on a commission or fee basis are under $250,000. It also allows the Department of Agriculture to accept electronic funds transfers and other quick payment methods as ways to meet the prompt payment rules for livestock purchases.

who_it_affects.group: Livestock marketing agencies that sell animals online or by video on a commission or fee basis
who_it_affects.how: They are treated as covered marketing agencies under the Packers and Stockyards Act if their average annual electronic sales exceed $250,000.

who_it_affects.group: Small electronic livestock sellers with average annual electronic sales under $250,000
who_it_affects.how: They are not counted as marketing agencies under this definition, so they fall outside this part of the Act.

who_it_affects.group: Livestock buyers and sellers who use electronic payment systems
who_it_affects.how: Electronic funds transfers and other fast payment methods approved by the Department of Agriculture can be used to meet prompt payment requirements for livestock purchases.

when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was enacted on October 7, 2016, though the Department of Agriculture's decisions about which payment methods count are made separately.
